corrected_value.title: Involuntary attentional capture is determined by task set: evidence from event-related brain potentials.

decision.quote: Previous studies have shown that cues in the target color capture attention, whereas neutral cues do not ( Eimer and Kiss, 2008 ; Lien et al., 2008 ). We hope to replicate this result in the present study.
decision.reason: No prior adjudication or state file existed for this work. In Experiment 1, the authors explicitly set out to replicate Eimer and Kiss (2008) by testing whether target-color (go) cues elicit an N2pc component and behavioral cueing benefits while neutral cues do not, and they directly compare and confirm this ERP capture finding in the Experiment 1 Results/Discussion and General Discussion. Shipped row 2426 (Anderson & Folk, 2012, 10.3758/s13414-012-0325-9) is a purely behavioral study of go/nogo cueing costs and is a distinct work from Eimer and Kiss (2008) and sibling targets.

corrected_value.authors: Eimer, M., Kiss, M., Press, C., Sauter, D.
corrected_value.title: The roles of feature-specific task set and bottom-up salience in attentional capture: an ERP study.

decision.quote: Previously, Eimer et al. (2009) had observed an enhanced N2 component in response to color-cues that did not match the target cues. Thus, the most straightforward prediction is that an enhanced N2 occurs for neutral and nogo cues alike because both do not match the go-color.
decision.reason: No prior adjudication or state file existed for this work. Experiment 1 formulates a direct prediction from Eimer et al.'s (2009) spatial-cueing ERP finding of an enhanced anterior N2 to non-matching color cues relative to target-matching color cues, empirically tests cue-related ERPs at Fz for non-matching (neutral and nogo) versus matching (go) cues in Results, and explicitly compares the observed anterior negativity against Eimer et al. (2009) in the Discussion and General Discussion. This 2009 JEP:HPP article is distinct from shipped row 2426 (Anderson & Folk, 2012) and from the 2008 N2pc studies in targets 1 and 2.

corrected_value.authors: Diener, E., Tay, L., & Myers, D. G.
corrected_value.title: The religion paradox: If religion makes people happy, why are so many dropping out?

decision.quote:
Study 1 was a direct replication of previous cross-cultural research on the religiosity-

adjustment relation. Yet, this study differed from previous research in three important ways.

First, previous research operationalized psychological adjustment as life satisfaction

(Stavrova et al., 2013), subjective well-being (Diener et al., 2011), depression (Leurent et al.,

2013), or social self-esteem (Gebauer et al., 2012b). From an RASV perspective, however,

global self-esteem is the most appropriate adjustment indicator.
decision.reason: Addressing the prior parent review objection: the paper explicitly states that its studies examine the replicability of prior evidence for cross-cultural differences in the religiosity-adjustment relation and describes Study 1 as a replication of prior cross-cultural research including Diener, Tay, & Myers (2011), which found in Gallup World Poll data that religious adjustment benefits (subjective well-being) were restricted to religious countries (r = .10-.20). Re-testing this cross-cultural moderation with global self-esteem (and also testing the Gallup World Poll country-level religiosity index in Note 10 and interpersonal-contact controls in Study 3) is an explicit conceptual replication. Diener et al. (2011) is completely distinct from shipped row 405 (Gebauer et al., 2013d / corrected to Gebauer, Sedikides, & Neberich, 2012b) and sibling targets 2 and 3.
